changed_views: Patel explicitly changes from expecting superintelligence at least the better part of a decade away to a 2028 median for AI-researcher parity and expert-level capability across fields by 2030; these are his forecasts, with a substantial late tail.

He retracts much of his earlier claim that weight-updating continual learning must precede research automation, now favoring much longer effective context and the possibility of automating the research that solves learning itself. Existing context-compression studies do not settle that question.

Relative to prior coverage of Navier-Stokes on September 9 and CoBench on August 22, the new value is Patel's revised causal argument and the November METR assessment. The mathematical result and benchmark are not new discoveries in this episode.

The primary sources support separating accelerating assisted research from autonomous replacement: supervised task leadership, retrospective diagnosis and mathematical search each provide narrower evidence than the full research-automation thesis.
follow_ups: Track independent updates to METR's acceleration estimate, with uncertainty, changes in task mix and evidence separating AI assistance from compute, data and other organizational changes.
Measure whether automated research improves end-to-end frontier training outcomes per unit of experiment compute and human supervision, including unsuccessful experiments and integration failures.

Look for prospective tests that train research agents on historical problems and then evaluate new frontier work, holding out tasks and checking whether small-model improvements survive at the actual deployment scale.

Require multiweek or multimonth on-the-job learning results before treating long-context compression as solved continual learning; separately measure transfer from simulated environments into real organizations.
For synthetic task pipelines, track verifier errors, contaminated holdouts, human-input dependence and gains on independent evaluations as model-generated tasks become a larger share of training.

Revisit the compute scenario using delivered hardware, utilization and the fraction allocated to experiments; compare marginal research output from another agent with output from more experiment compute.

signals.claim: Patel cites METR's estimate of roughly doubled progress at Anthropic as evidence that AI-assisted research is already accelerating model development; the underlying reports retain substantial uncertainty and human supervision.
signals.evidence: The [November 5 METR assessment](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/) estimates about 2x progress on well-specified tasks, with 1.3x or 3x both plausible, and judges that most current acceleration likely comes from AI. It distinguishes that subjective causal judgment from a 1.9x AECI trend estimate, notes extensive evidence redactions and says contributions remain primarily assisted. Patel also cites Claude leading 26% of R&D work by August, up from under 1% in February. [Anthropic's definition](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development) means completing most of a task from a high-level prompt under human supervision; the measured fully autonomous share was zero. These are stronger indicators than coding-agent expenditure alone, but neither establishes that entire researcher jobs or frontier model-development cycles have been automated.

signals.claim: Patel moves his median forecast for matching the best human AI researchers to 2028, partly because he now thinks extended in-context learning could overcome the memory bottleneck, while retaining at least a 25% chance of reaching that milestone only after 2032.
signals.evidence: His forecast assumes labs continue at full speed without voluntary or government slowdowns. He previously expected a much longer path and considered missing continual learning a major obstacle; now he argues that months-long effective sessions or automated research into learning algorithms could suffice. This remains a hypothesis: the linked [Cartridges paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266) studies offline-trained context representations and benchmark improvements, not months of successful on-the-job learning. His mathematical analogy also needs qualification. [OpenAI's September 8 announcement](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/) reports a forced Navier-Stokes counterexample from an internal multiagent system, with human decisions about resource allocation and follow-up prompts; the 88-hour search was followed by 17 hours of formalization. That company-reported result, already covered in the September 9 digest, is background for Patel's extrapolation, not independent proof of autonomous AI-research scaling or a new November discovery.

signals.claim: Patel argues that verifiable objectives across pretraining, post-training and inference can train research agents and coordinate parallel work; the critical unresolved step is transferring local benchmark gains into better frontier models.
signals.evidence: His proposed objectives include compute needed to reach a held-out loss, data needed to learn a new environment, and latency or GPU utilization. He suggests training agents to predict whether improvements at 100 million parameters survive at 10 billion; this is a proposed research-taste environment. The [nanoGPT speedrun](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt) demonstrates a bounded competition targeting a specified validation loss on eight H100s. [Anthropic's CoBench description](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/f61d49fa5596956a5dec75fea0e973bf6a6a8378/Redacted%20Risk%20Report%20August%202026%20.pdf) specifies 449 difficulty-filtered historical root-cause problems, largely from February-April, graded against known solutions; it does not establish deployment of Patel's proposed RL loop. [Magic's pretraining report](https://magic.dev/blog/pretraining), which he also cites, explicitly says many improvements to tiny models fail at larger scale and describes testing changes across multiple scales. These sources support measurable subproblems while leaving end-to-end research judgment and transfer unproven.

signals.claim: Patel argues that data need not remain an externally supplied bottleneck because models can improve the pipelines that construct and verify their next training tasks; DeepSeek offers a concrete, bounded example of that mechanism.
signals.evidence: He points to automated filtering, synthetic data and RL-environment construction as research work that can itself be optimized against measured outcomes. Section 5.1 of the linked [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash report](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.19969) says the release retained established SFT, RL and on-policy-distillation methods and attributes essentially all observed post-training gains to better synthesized data and environments. It describes training task constructors on difficulty and correctness, plus re-auditing tasks using subsequent rollout evidence. The same report says task construction remains imperfect and describes inputs from employee and partner workflows. This is a developer-reported training pipeline, not evidence that human feedback has disappeared or that self-generated environments will cover every domain. The potentially consequential shift is that part of the data bottleneck becomes an automatable engineering and verification problem.

signals.claim: Patel assigns equal odds to a compute-limited burst of three to six years of AI progress in one year and to a software-only singularity; his mechanism relies on cheaper, better-designed experiments, not a demonstrated elimination of compute constraints.
signals.evidence: In his burst scenario, diminishing returns eventually require more chips and datacenters. He proposes substituting abundant agent labor for wasteful experiments and learning more from small runs. The [GPT-4 technical report](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.08774) supports one narrow precedent: predicting final held-out code loss from similarly trained models using up to 10,000x less compute; it does not show that arbitrary new research ideas transfer. His numerical compute argument is conditional on continued quadrupling. The [written essay's footnote 16](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/rsi) qualifies the audio's nearly 10,000 agents each running a GPT-3-sized experiment daily: the projected whole end-2027 fleet supports about 7,660 such runs per day, and allocating one-third to experiments gives each of 10,000 agents roughly one run every four days. These are scenario calculations, not announced fleet capacity, measured utilization or agent research productivity.

summary: In this solo essay, Dwarkesh Patel advances his median date for AI systems matching the best human AI researchers to 2028 and expects expert-level capability across fields by 2030. His consequential argument is that verifiable research objectives, automated training-data production and cheaper experiments could turn current researcher assistance into a compounding development loop. METR's assessment supplies evidence of acceleration inside Anthropic, but the dates, magnitude of a subsequent takeoff and transfer to general expertise remain Patel's forecasts. Mathematical results and historical-task benchmarks do not establish autonomous frontier research or economy-wide deployment.
why_it_matters: The useful update is a testable account of where AI development could accelerate: research automation, data generation, sample efficiency and experiment design. It also identifies what would keep compute scarce even after labor becomes abundant. The assessment supports watching measured research throughput and frontier-scale transfer; it does not establish Patel's timelines, unlimited returns to agent swarms or the disappearance of physical infrastructure constraints.
